X500001.text_comments: 1: The significance of the number 1,40, as well as of 2,10 in line 3, is unknown to me; for a suggestion of J. Steele, see p. 392. A similar number occurs in No. 2 I 1´. 2: the sign after ád is certainly not ŠÚ. I translate GAR here by "it (i.e. the moon) made", assuming a form of sakānu like iškun or iltakan. In Iater, more detailed eclipse reports, a time interval is given with GAR, and a translation "onset", i.e. the first part of the eclipse, is appropriate in these cases. 3: 2,10 is written on the edge. 9: The almost completely broken sign at the end of the line has an upper horizontal wedge and so cannot be GAR.
X500001.date_comments: Date (J. M. Steele): This tablet contains four observations of successive lunar eclipses observed in the accession, 1st and 2nd years of an unknown reign. They are followed by two predictions for years 2 and 3. In LBAT this tablet was dated to the reign of Nabonassar; however, there are problems with this date. For example, the fourth eclipse, which would be on -745 July 21, probably rose after the end of totality and so it is doubtful if the total phase could have been seen. Between -850 and -310 (after which accession years were not used), the only other possible date for this tablet would be for the series of eclipses starting with -800 January 4. However, this would lead to an implausibly early date for the beginning of the year, and so I am forced to tentatively follow LBAT in accepting the eclipse series beginning with -746 February 6.

X500002.tablet_comments: Lunar eclipses and eclipse possibilities, arranged in 18-year groups. For a discussion, see Appendix, and C. B. F. Walker, in Mesopotamia and Iran in the Persian Period: Conquest and Imperialism 539-331 BC, ed J. Curtis (London 1997) 17-25.
X500002.text_comments: Obv. I 1´: The significance of the number at the beginning of the line is obscure to me; for a suggestion of J. Steele, see p. 392. There are similar numbers in No. 1:1 and 3. II 2´: a is abbreviated from E-a = uṣâ "it came out". 1/2 ḪAB fits the size of the lunar eclipse of -712 April 19, but the time does not fit; the moon had already risen when the eclipse began. Possibly ana ŠÚ šámaš "before sunset" is to be emended to GE6 GIN "after sunset". IV: According to the layout of the tablet, this should concern the eclipse of -676 May 11. Rev. II´ 7´: bi is an abbreviation of birīl. III´ 1´: this eclipse should be of -352 May 28. The partial lunar eclipse on that date however began only after the moon had set. A reading ME NIM would be appropriate, but the remaining traces look at most like ana ZÁLAG. This could be taken as abbreviation of GE6 ana ZÁLAG, but it still would have to be considered an error. III´ 8´: ÍB is abbreviated from ÍB-TAG4 = rēhtu. V´ 6´: 19 looks more like 20, but 19 agrees with the total in line 8. V´ 12´: this could be a reference to the death of Philip Arrhidaeus. The only thing certain (or at least probable), however, is that Philip is mentioned here. V´ 14´: the usual title of Antigonus is rab uqu, written logographicall as GAL ÉRINmeš. The first sign may be GAL as well as DUMU. The next one could be ÉRIN (although it looks more like PI), but the last is certainly RU.

X500003.tablet_comments: Lunar eclipses and eclipse possibilities, arranged in 18-year groups. For a discussion, see Appendix, and C. B. F. Walker, in Mesopotamia and Iran in the Persian Period: Conquest and Imperialism 539-331 BC, ed J. Curtis (London 1997) 17-25.
X500003.text_comments: Obv. I´ 2: The first preserved sign is most likely KAM, certainly not MU. In other instances in this text where year numbers are written, they are also not preceded by MU. Nor are royal names preceded by vertical wedges. I am therefore inclined to read "(Year) I of Bel-ibni", but have to admit that I do not know what is written before it. II´ 1: This line begins the eclipse report for -685 Apr 22. After the destruction of Babylon by Sennacherib, there was no king in Babylonia. In analogy to line 5 below, one could restore "3" at the beginning of the line. Thereafter, a king's name or its equivalent is expected, but I could not find a suitable reading. A possible reading bar-tú "revolt" is unlikely. II´ 5: "(Year) 5" seems to be counted from the conquest of Babylon by Sennacherib.
X500003.date_comments: For dates of the eclipses see Appendix.

X500004.tablet_comments: Reports of lunar eclipses and eclipse possibilities, arranged in 18-year groups. Five columns each are preserved on obverse and reverse. For a discussion, see Appendix, and C. B. F. Walker, in Mesopotamia and Iran in the Persian Period: Conquest and Imperialism 539-331 BC, ed. J. Curtis (London 1997) 17-25.
X500004.text_comments: Obv. I´ 1´: the last sign looks like a large A. It is not ME; cf. ME in rev. III´ 4f. II´ 1´: the reading is uncertain; but the eclipse did occur in Virgo. V´ 5´: the missing word at the end of the line may have meant "was missing". Whether two-thirds of the lunar disk were still outside the earth's shadow depends on visibility conditions near the horizon at the time. When the moon sank below the horizon, it was rather about two-thirds eclipsed. Rev. II´ 1´: 15 bēru may mean 15/60, i.e. one-fourth of this time-unit. There may be an error here, though, because usually these time intervals are given in degrees, and 15° (twice as much as one-four bēru) would better fit computation. An indication of direction is expected, cf. obv. IV´ 2´.
X500004.date_comments: For dates of the eclipses see Appendix.

X500005.tablet_comments: This tablet is clearly a copy of an older exemplar (see the remarks "new break" in Rev. II). It contains beside eclipses only a few other observations, but a number of events. A 16th and 19th year exclude all reigns of shorter duration. The eclipses and the historical remarks suffice to date the contents to the reign of Nabopolassar (for details, see below).
X500005.text_comments: Obv. I 7´f.: I do not know above what the moon was during the eclipse, nor what was 6 fingers from Jupiter. II 12´: since what happened to the "bright star of constellation [.. .]" is not preserved one cannot guess which star it is. Rev. I 3´: I do not understand the signs after UGU; they may all be one place name. II: the first six lines begin (in their preserved part) with the word "new break" which indicate that the original from which this tablet was copied, was damaged here. It is difficult to estimate the size of the gaps, but some considerations can be offered. Of the description of the moon only lines 1 and 2 are left. 1 2/3 bēru could be the time of the eclipse, i.e. of its beginning. lf GE6 is read correctly, it should be followed (in the break) by either GIN or ana ZÁLAG, i.e. resulting in either "after sunset" or "before sunrise". 3: Mars and Venus must have been visible or have become visible during the eclipse; the appropriate words are lost in the left part of line 4. 4f.: the only star near the ecliptic called a "foot" is the "rear foot of the Lion", β Virginis. This leads to a restoration [ár šá mulUR]-GU-LA in the following line. The following word, KUR, here probably means "to rise". So one could assume that Jupiter rose behind β Vir. What however is to be made of the following "8° to Regulus"? If Jupiter is close to β Vir, it cannot be 8° from Regulus. What is at approximately this distance from Regulus is the moon (λ 103°). lt is however unusual to give an indication of the moon's position among the planets. If these words do refer to the moon, the word lost in the break was probably adir "is was eclipsed". 6: the words "the remainder of the planets" is always followed in eclipse reports by "did not stand there"; this restoration is therefore certain. Unfortunately, one cannot tell how many of the planets were invisible. 7f.: I cannot read the first preserved sign(s) in line 7; but it does not fit the phrase "did not stand there" which is expected to continue line 6. The word for thunder, literally "Cry of Adad", is spread over lines 7 and 8; there was nothing written in the left part of line 8.
X500005.date_comments: Date (J. M. Steele): A year 19 is mentioned in Rev. I, 6´ thus excluding reigns of shorter duration. In year 16 of this reign, a lunar eclipse was observed in month VI. Between -750 and 100, the only reign to have lasted for at least 19 years and to have had an observable lunar eclipse in month VI of year 16 is Nabopolassar. This is sufficient information to date the eclipse in Obv. II´, 7´-15´ to -609 September 15. Obv. I, 4´-10´ contains a report of a lunar eclipse that, from the months listed in Obv. I, 11´-17´, must have occurred at least a year before the eclipse in Obv. II´, 7´- I5´. Given this restriction, the next preceding eclipse visible in Babylon was on -611 November 5. The observed details of the eclipse, so far as they are preserved, are in agreement with this date and Jupiter was indeed stationary around that time. The eclipse described in Rev. II, 1-7 is most likely that of -605 January 8. Jupiter rose just before the beginning of the eclipse, but was still close to the horizon when the eclipse began, and so could well have not been noticed until later: It also rose slightly after the 'rear foot of the Lion' (β Virginis) (cf. Rev. II, 4-5). All of the other planets were below the horizon at the time of the eclipse (cf. Rev. II, 6-7) and so I am unable to explain why Mars and Venus are mentioned in Rev. II, 3. However, there are no other eclipses which give a better fit within the plausible date range for this column of the tablet (say Nabopolassar 19, 20, or 21).

X500006.tablet_comments: Reports of lunar eclipses, reign of Nebukadnezar Il.
X500006.text_comments: I 3: the sign transliterated as 5 looks like šá. II 1f.: Eclipse of -594 Nov 27. The moon rose eclipsed. 2/3 bēru could refer to the time until the end of the eclipse. 9: Here too, 1 bēru 10° is the time from moonrise to the end of the eclipse. III 12: the tablet has šá PA instead of 4 ZÁLAG.
X500006.date_comments: For the dates of the eclipses, see Appendix.

X500007.text_comments: II´ 1´: The signs in the beginning of the preserved part look like 45 if the wedges do belong together in this way; the line would begin rather far to the left. The eclipse of -562 Mar 13 was not visible in Babylon. But even then, a computed time might be given in the text.
X500007.date_comments: For the dates of the eclipses, see Appendix. Date (J. M. Steele): A year 42 is mentioned in II´, 2´, thus excluding reigns of shorter duration. Between -750 and 100, only the reigns of Nebukadnezar II and Artaxerxes II and the Seleucid Era lasted that long. Only for Nebukadnezar II were there eclipses visible in months VI and XII of year 42.

X500008.text_comments: Obv. I 13´: J. Steele suggests the eclipse of -528 Nov 17 here. The traces of the month name do not fit the reading APIN well, but GAN is not better. Rev. I 10: the moon was near η Piscium. II: three beginnings of lines are visible; the second and third of them am covered by an intrusion from the left. This shows that the left column was inscribed first.
X500008.date_comments: For the dates of the eclipses, see Appendix. Date (J. M. Steele): Intercalary months VI2 in the third year of a reign are only attested for Cambyses and Darius I. Only during Cambyses' reign was there an eclipse visible in month VI of year 4.

X500009.tablet_comments: Both fragments are part of the same tablet but cannot be joined. Reports of lunar eclipses, arranged in 18-year groups. Columns continue from obverse onto reverse.
X500009.text_comments: Obv. 2: Note that ina 2 i also occurs in rev. III´ 9. Its meaning is unclear to me; "in/at the second (time?)" does not make sense. 1,8 here should be a time interval as in rev. III´ 9. It would fit the time "after sunset" (GE6 GIN) for the beginning of the eclipse of -409 Dec 21. 6´: Eclipse of -408 Jun 16. Only the very last minutes of this eclipse were visible in Babylon. Only the general area where the moon was is given in the report. If the translation "and it cleared" of u ZÁLAG is correct, these words would continue the expression "after sunset", of which the literal translation is "the night went". 7´: The sign SUD occurs in eclipse reports to describe the color of the eclipsed moon. I do not understand the rest of the line. 12´: The first part of the line up to the separation sign (represented in the transliteration by :::) belongs to the preceding column. The traces after GUBme may be an erasure. Rev. I´ 1´-3´: Overflow into col. II´. II´: 1´-3´: These lines contain overflow from col. 1´. 4´f.: Eclipse of -423 Sep 28/29. Note that "after sunset" is represented here and in line 10´ just by GIN instead of GE6 GlN. 10´f.: Eclipse of -420 Feb 2. A total duration of 64° is compatible with this eclipse. III´ 1-3: Eclipse of -424 Apr 15, overflow from column to the left. Only part of line 1 refers to the eclipse of -406 Apr 26. 5: all readings in this line are uncertain. 7f.: The ends of lines 7-9 copied in LBAT are now broken off. 8´: I cannot read what was mentioned before Jupiter among the visible planets. Its second part looks like ḪAR. Since Jupiter is always mentioned first, and only the planets mentioned were visible during the eclipse, the unclear sign can not be the name of a planet. Maybe it qualified the eclipse in some way. The same sign(s) may also have occurred at the beginning of line 10´ where only the end of the sign is preserved. 9´: ina 2 i also occurs in obv. 2.
X500009.date_comments: For the dates of the eclipses, see Appendix.

X500010.copy: 37652 is listed as LBAT *1429. The piece 37088 was brought to my attention by C. B. F. Walker.
X500010.tablet_comments: Reports of lunar eclipses, arranged in 18-year groups.
X500010.text_comments: l´ 1´-2´: Eclipse of -382 Dec 23. The moon was in Cancer; this partial eclipse began before sunrise, and the moon set before it was over. The half broken sign in line 2´ could be [NI]M, but this would lead to a restoration [ME NI]M, i.e. after sunrise, which is not correct for this eclipse. 5´-7´: α Geminorum restored according to computation. II´ 1´-3´: Eclipse of -363 Jan 2. The reading [ZÁL]AG is a guess; C. B. F. Walker reads [M]E. Reading 2,30 ("left side") follows his suggestion. 10´: the last sign in this line may be part of another column to the right.
X500010.date_comments: For the dates of the eclipses, see Appendix. Date (J. M. Steele): BM 37652: From ll´, 4´-6´, eclipses were visible in months III and IX of regnal year 41. The only possibility is Artaxerxes II. BM 37088: Assuming that the damaged year number in line 4 is 33, 43, or 53, the only possible dates that would fit the months of the eclipse possibilities are Artaxerxes II 42-43 or SE 32-33. The latter can be discounted on the basis of BM 48090 which contains consecutive lunar eclipse possibilities for SE 32ff. that differ markedly for the reports given in this text. This only leaves Artaxerxes II 42-43. The computed circumstances of this eclipse agree well with those recorded in the text. After this text had been dated, it was found to join BM 37652.

X500011.tablet_comments: Solar eclipse possibilities. This tablet was brought to my attention by C. B . F. Walker. He makes the following remarks: The identification of Obverse and Reverse is not altogether certain. The narrowing thickness of the fragment shows that it comes from near to either the top right or bottom left corner of the tablet. The present tentative identification of the Obverse as such is guided by the way in which the columns on Obverse and Reverse appear to line up, and by doubts whether there would be room for the additional column that would be required on what is now identified as Obverse if the Obverse and Reverse were switched. If this understanding of the tablet is correct then the 5-month interval and the transition from Obverse to Reverse mirror exactly the lay-out of the so-called "Solar Saros" (LBAT 1430), published by Aaboe et al., in TAPS 81/6 (1991), 25-31. This in turn suggests that the present table ended with the solar eclipse possibility of Antigonus year 5, month VI2 (-312 Oct 16). Given the relative infrequency of observed solar eclipses, the small script employed and the very compressed format of this tablet, it seems possible that the entire 18-year cycle was contained on a single tablet. It also seems possible that with 12 eclipse cycles on each side (not impossible), this tablet might have covered the time-span from Nabonassar to Antigonus in the same manner as the group LBAT 1414, 1415-1417 and 1419, appear to do for lunar eclipses. There are two "firing-holes" on the Obverse.
X500011.text_comments: II´ obv. 1´: the change of reign mentioned here (from Artaxerxes II to Artaxerxes III) must have taken place before the solar eclipse possibility of March 11, 358 BC. III´ rev. 6: reading ME NIM suggested by computation. III´ rev. 9f.: according to this note, the change of reign from Artaxerxes III Ochos to Arses took place in month VI, i.e. between August 26 and September 25, 338 BC.

X500012.tablet_comments: Lunar data. One side contains Lunar Six, the other side lunar and solar eclipses. Probably same tablet as BM 37276, which is near the right edge of the original tablet. Obv. and Rev. uncertain; tentatively, the eclipses were assigned to the reverse.
X500012.date_comments: Date (J. M. Steele): BM 36612: Column II´ reports three successive eclipse observations, the third of which occurred in month X of a year 10. During the first eclipse, Saturn was seen to set. During the second, at least two planets were not seen, and during the final eclipse, more than one-fourth of the disk was covered. The only trio of eclipses fulfilling these circumstances between -750 and 100 are -326 January 14, -326 July 9 and -325 January 3, in years 9 and 10 of Alexander. The eclipse on -362 January 14 was total with Saturn setting during the eclipse. The -326 July 9 eclipse rose shortly before its end. The eclipse on -325 January 3 was total; however, it did not rise until after the end of totality. After this text had been dated, it was found to join BM 37043 + 37107.

X500013.tablet_comments: Probably same tablet as No. 12 ( BM 36612+37043+37107), BM 37276 is a piece at the right edge. Lunar data; one side contains Lunar Six, the other eclipses. Of the Lunar Six, two columns are missing between the two pieces, because Darius III year 5, which is dealt with in column V´ or No. 12, corresponds to Alexander year 6. Obv. and Rev. uncertain; tentatively, the eclipses were assigned to the reverse.

X500014.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of -283 March 17.
X500014.text_comments: 6´ The last sign looks like ŠE, not GÍR.
X500014.date_comments: Date (J. M. Steele): On the date of this eclipse the moon was near to α Virginis. During the eclipse Saturn was visible; Sirius set during onset. The only eclipse fulfilling these conditions is that of -283 March 17.

X500015.tablet_comments: Lunar eclipses. There are traces of a column to the left of the preserved text.
X500015.date_comments: For the dates of the eclipses, see Appendix. Date J. M. Steele: From 4´, an eclipse was seen in month III of a year 33. Between -750 and 100, the only eclipse visible in Babylon in month III or a year 33 is that on -278, June 19, during the Seleucid Era.

X500016.text_comments: Obv. II´ 4´: the "4 stars of its breast" are α, γ, η, ζ Leonis. Rev.: the order of columns cannot be determined with certainty. II´ 3´: A Diary (No. -160A) is preserved for this eclipse, and it gives "48 GE6 GIN" for the beginning of the eclipse. Here, the left part of the first sign is damaged and only partly visible; it ends with two oblique wedges. The oblique wedges are clearly two, not three. Nevertheless, one could assume copying error for in 48.
X500016.date_comments: For dates of the eclipses, see Appendix.

X500017.text_comments: Obv.: The year number in LBAT (SE 127) does not agree with the eclipses available. In SE 127, eclipses were in months II and VIII. In SE 117, eclipses were in months III and VIII; the one in month III was only penumbral and occurred in daytime; the time given in line 2 agrees more or less with the computed daytime for this eclipse; however, the reading is not certain. It can be restored from the Goal-year text LBAT 1249 rev. I 8´f., referring to SE 117: SIG 13 AN-KU10 sin šá DIB in 15 ME ana ŠÚ šámaš. In a Diary for SE 117 (No. -194A), the entry is AN-KU10 sin BAR DIB in 15 ME ana ŠÚ šamáš. The eclipse in month VIII was not visible either; not much seems to have been reported in the text, which at least does not contradict the proposed date. The day number 15 agrees: - 194 Nov 15/16 = SE 117 VIII 15. This eclipse too is preserved in LBAT 1249 rev. I 10´, which gives APIN GE6 15 etc. Rev.: The year number was read SE 124 in LBAT. There was no observable lunar eclipse in Babylon in this year. A reading SE 134 seems possible (the tablet is slightly damaged here). The eclipse of -177 Jul 12/13 began (20.03 UT) when β Cygni culminated, so this reading is very probable. The relation between the entries remains problematic: if obverse and reverse are identified correctly, one would expect that the eclipses immediately follow each other; if the sides are reversed, a later eclipse is followed by an earlier one.

X500018.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 121 XII 15 = -189 Feb. 28.
X500018.text_comments: 3: I owe the reading of the star name to P. J. Huber. 8: reading of the end of this line proposed by P. J. Huber.

X500019.tablet_comments: Report of solar eclipse of -189 Mar 14.

X500020.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 157 XII 15 = - 153 Mar 21.

X500021.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 183 VIII 13 = -128 Nov 5.

X500022.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 192 II 14 = -119, June I.

X500023.copy: LBAT 1334 (34963), 1435 (35198), 1443 (35238); an unnumbered piece was joined to this tablet by I.L. Finkel
X500023.tablet_comments: Eclipse reports and some lunar data, preserved for -88 to -86. The columns are numbered with the assumption that there were four columns on each side. The columns on the reverse go from right to left.
X500023.text_comments: Most of these comments are by Christopher Walker, who studied this tablet after he had made the join of BM 34963 with BM 35198+35238. Not more than one or two lines (if any) are lost at the end of the reverse. III´ 7´f.: probably lunar eclipse of -88 Mar 21. IV´ 6´ ff.: lunar eclipse of -88 Sep 15. V´1´ff.: solar eclipse of -88 Sep 29. VI´ 19´: probably beginning of solar eclipse of -87 Aug 20. VII´ 5´f.: solar eclipse of -86 Feb 14. VII´ 9´ff.: lunar eclipse of -86 Feb 28. The text agrees with the Diary No. -87C rev. 18´.

X500024.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 231 I 14 = -80 Apr 21.
X500024.text_comments: In line 4, restore possibly, ŠUDUN [ANŠE]; this ziqpu star was identified by J. Schaumberger as η or υ Boötis.

X500025.copy: J.N. Strassmaier, ZA 3 ( 1888) 147f. Listed as LBAT **1445.
X500025.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 232 I 13 = -79 Apr 10/11.

X500026.text_comments: Eclipse of -79 Oct 5. The time given fits the beginning of the eclipse; the nearest Normal star was α Arietis. Obv. 4: reading based on collation by G. R. F. Assar.

X500027.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 244 X 15 = -66 Jan 19. Duplicate of No. 28.

X500028.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 244 X 15 = -66 Jan 19. Duplicate of No. 27.

X500029.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 245 X 14 = -65 Jan 8.

X500030.tablet_comments: Report of lunar eclipse of SE 246 IX 14 = -65 Dec 28.

X500031.tablet_comments: Report of solar eclipse, probably of -9 Jun 30.
X500031.text_comments: This report on a large solar eclipse shows several unusual features. It also contains contradictory elements in its observations.
X500031.date_comments: Date (J. M. Steele): During this eclipse, Venus and Mercury were visible. Sirius was in its period of non-visibility, that is it was not visible during the night. However, it was seen during the eclipse. This implies that the eclipse was very large, probably having a magnitude of more than 0.95. This is sufficient information to date this eclipse to -9 June 30. For full details of the dating of this eclipse, see J. M. Steele, The Latest Dated Astronomical Observation from Babylon, in A. R. Millard (ed.), Archaeological Sciences '97, British Archaeological Reports. Oxford (forthcoming).

X500032.tablet_comments: Fragment of eclipse report; it was brought to my attention by I. L. Finkel. The script of this fragment is exceptionally small.
X500032.text_comments: 7´: at the end of the line, either Mars (AN) or Venus (dele-bat) can be restored.

X500033.text_comments: In spite of its bad state of preservation, this text ought to be datable; I have not succeeded so far. Legible year numbers occur only in Rev. II. Obv. 11´, 13´, 15´, 18´: At the beginning of these lines, almost at the edge, there are damaged signs. One could expect year numbers. In line 11´ the sign could be 10. Whatever is written in line 13´ is certainly no number at all. In line 15´ there are some oblique wedges; in line 18´, what remains could be the right part or 5, but need not be a number either. Obv. 13 ´: šamáš is written as a raised correction. Rev. 11´: The space for this column is marked on the tablet by three parallel vertical lines. Only the upper part or the column is inscribed. 2´: 22 is written over another number. 4´: The reading of the first signs is uncertain; it is based on a partial lunar eclipse which occurred in SE 75 month VI in Pisces. 6´: In the beginning one expects a month name; the traces could be those of ZÍZ (month XI). They do not fit month XII which had an invisible lunar eclipse in SE 75.

X500034.copy: J. N. Strassmaier, ZA 7 (1892) 198-201: ZA 8 (1893) 106-7: T. Boiy, Laatachemenidisch en hellenistisch Babylon, pl. 2; Th. G. Pinches: PI. 11
X500034.text_comments: I owe the following remarks to C. B. F. Walker. The beginning of the text is broken away, and the preserved text begins at line 1´; however, if the chronological scheme is carried back to its maximum likely extent, then the cycle would begin with the first recorded eclipse of LBAT 1413, in month XII of the accession year of Nabû-naṣir; in 747 B.C. Lines 28´ to 32´ are written sideways and probably contain a lunar eclipse report. Line 32´ should be the last line on the tablet unless this section was written in a double column.
X500034.bibliography: Th. G . Pinches, PSBA 6, 204; F. X. Kugler, SSB II 364 n. 1.

X500035.tablet_comments: Years and months of lunar eclipse possibilities; the preserved part shows entries from -646 to -573. The dates can be established because each column is 18 years (or 223 months) distant from the next. The only pattern of regnal years fitting the year numbers preserved and the dates of eclipse possibilities is the one indicated in parentheses in the translation. The numbers associated with some of eclipses follow the function for eclipse magnitudes discussed by J. Britton, Cenlaurus 32 (1989) 33ff. and O. Neugebauer, HAMA 526f. The sign BE is used as in some texts froim the ACT material to indicate the impossibility of an eclipse (ACT p. 163).
X500035.text_comments: 14: only traces of a vertical wedge (or maybe two) survive; it could be [KI]N, i.e. month VI. But since the 14th year of Nebukadnezar was a leap year with XII2, one expects month V. The number following the month name could be more than 6.

X500036.tablet_comments: Lunar Six for -322 to -318. The columns continue from the obverse to the reverse.
X500036.text_comments: The preserved part of the tablet happens to begin with a change of reign: Alexander died on II 29, and was succeeded by Philip Arrhidaeus; the first entry is for III 1. II 21: 4 damaged; the Diary No. -321 r. 19´ has 7.
X500036.bibliography: F. R. Stephenson, Phil. Trans. Royal Soc. London 276 ( 1974) 118-121.

X500039.tablet_comments: This text was described by A. Sachs in JCS 6 110-112. It contains the length of the months, the calendar date of the day (after full moon) when the moon set for the first time after sunrise, and the calendar date of the last visibility of the moon towards as the end of the month, for the years SE 62-93. These data are written in five columns on the obverse and three on the reverse. In addition, the tablet contains solstices, equinoxes, and Sirius data for the years SE 62-69. This material is written on the left edge and in the last section of each of the five columns of the obverse. In the translation, Roman numbers represent month names; "the 30" after a month name means that the preceding month had 29 days, "the 1st", that it had 30 days. This abbreviated "translation" is meant to save space and to represent the layout of the tablet.
X500039.text_comments: I do not know the significance of a horizontal wedge (transliterated "ina") before day numbers in lines I 21, 35, III 7, 21, 29, 40, IV 17, 36, VI 24, VII 10, 20, VIII 2, 31, and 34.

X500040.tablet_comments: Lunar data for SE 69 to 72 etc. = -242/1 to -239/8 etc.; the first section contains the sums of ŠÚ+NA and ME+GE6 for the second half of the year preceding the rest of the text, as in Goal-year Texts. The tablet was therefore probably used to prepare such texts.

X500041.tablet_comments: Lunar Six for SE 104 = -207/6 and other years.

X500042.tablet_comments: Lunar Six for SE 124. Tablet in the Morgan Library Collection at Yale University.
X500042.text_comments: If the numbers 2,5 in the last column are a year number, the preceding data should concern year 2,4, i.e., SE 124. The few preserved month lengths agree with computation for this year. VI 8-11: The sequence of time intervals as noted is impossible. Maybe they were entemd in the wrong order.

X500046.tablet_comments: Lunar Six for three years. Columns continue from obverse to reverse.

X500047.text_comments: A meaningful translation is not possible. The remaining words may belong to eclipses or other lunar data.

X500048.tablet_comments: Lunar Six. Vertical rulings to make three columns.

X500049.tablet_comments: Lunar Six for at least 3 years. Columns continue from obverse to lower edge to reverse.
X500049.text_comments: Obv. I 17: at the end, GE6 is expected, but the traces are illegible to me. Rev. I 6´: it seems that the interval "moonset to sunrise" was observed both on the 12th and the 13th, similar to obv. I 14-19, but no number is recorded for the 13th. The reading of the signs following "13" is uncertain. They look like two small ŠÚ-signs. Rev. II 5´-8´: the time intervals do not fit the times of the day: ŠÚ and na belong to daytime, ME and GE6 to nighttime.

X500052.tablet_comments: I´: Saturn; II´: Approaches of Mars and Mercury.
X500052.text_comments: This tablet contains events in the 7th century and does not yet use the rigid terminology of later texts. I´: the sections in this column cannot refer to concecutive years, because Saturn's movement is not fast enough to reach Virgo from α Leonis within less than a year (lines 11´-12´). Similarly, lines 2´ and 3´ cannot belong to adjacent years. II´: 1: Ḫumbaḫaldašu year 8 = -680/679. A conjunction of Mars and Mercury occurred on -680 Sep 7/8. 2´: Esarhaddon year 2 III 16 corresponds to -678 Jun 3 according to the tables in Parpola, LAS II. A conjunction of Mars and Mercury (and of Jupiter) occurred a few days later, on -678 Jun 9. 5´: Šamaš-šum-ukīn year 17 II 19 = -650 Apr 28. Mercury became visible about Apr 22, Mars became invisible about May 9. 8´: Mars was above Mercury on the day indicated, but not as much as 14 fingers. 11´: the day number in the date is no longer preserved. The traces of the month name fit either DU6 (month VII) or KIN (month VI) but there was no conjunction of Mars and Mercury in these months; there was a conjunction in month V (-618 Aug I). Nabopolassar is written as Aplaja also in Rev. 7.

X500053.text_comments: This tablet contains events in the 7th century and does not yet use the rigid terminology of later texts. Side A I´: the sections in this column cannot refer to concecutive years, because Saturn's movement is not fast enough to reach Virgo from α Leonis within less than a year (lines 11´-12´). Similarly, lines 2´ and 3´ cannot belong to adjacent years. II´: 1: Ḫumbaḫaldašu year 8 = -680/679. A conjunction of Mars and Mercury occurred on -680 Sep 7/8. 2´: Esarhaddon year 2 III 16 corresponds to -678 Jun 3 according to the tables in Parpola, LAS II. A conjunction of Mars and Mercury (and of Jupiter) occurred a few days later, on -678 Jun 9. 5´: Šamaš-šum-ukīn year 17 II 19 = -650 Apr 28. Mercury became visible about Apr 22, Mars became invisible about May 9. 8´: Mars was above Mercury on the day indicated, but not as much as 14 fingers. 11´: the day number in the date is no longer preserved. The traces of the month name fit either DU6 (month VII) or KIN (month VI) but there was no conjunction of Mars and Mercury in these months; there was a conjunction in month V (-618 Aug I). Nabopolassar is written as Aplaja also in Rev. 7. Side B II´ 1: traces of two small verticals remain of the year number, so it may have been 15 or 18. 3-5: Year 19 in a section before one on Nabopolassar is most likely Kandalanu. But in all of this year (-628/7) Mars was not in Scorpius. The next possibility is Šamas-šum-ukīn. An event is recorded for IX 2 which corresponds to -648 Nov 13. On this date, Mars was close to α Librae. Unfortunately, I cannot read the times of line 3 with certainty. The next date, day 28, mentions Mars before the "two small stars of the ear of the Scorpion". These stars are so far unidentified; but on the corresponding date, -648 Dec 9, Mars was just before the two stars ω1 and ω2 Scorpii. The next day, it passed the two stars at a very short distance; it was morning star and therefore rose with them. The remark "they entered each other" I take to mean that it was impossible to distinguish between Mars and (one of) the two stars which are of magnitude 6. 7: computation shows Mars near α Tauri; restore šá GU4- AN or similar at the end of the line. 9: this entry is more or less correct, but not in chronological sequence. 10: Mars was above α Tauri; maybe šá ÙLU is to be restored. 12: if the month name is in fact IZI, the position of Mars is more than 10° east of β Virginis.

X500054.tablet_comments: Obv.: Mercury; Rev.: Venus, according to A. Sachs in LBAT for -586/85, -585/84 etc. Both the dates of the Greek-letter phenomena and the positions do not agree very well with a date in the reign of Nebukadnezar II, but other reigns are even worse. The main problem is in col. III´, that year 20 of Nebukanezar did not have an intercalary Addaru while the text has it; and that year 21 had an intercalary Ululu which is not mentioned in the text. Therefore, the year number 21 in line 10´ may have been misread. In JHA 23 (1992) 199, N. A. Roughton and G. L. Canzoneri state that they were unable to find a date for the Venus data on this tablet.

X500055.tablet_comments: Jupiter: Top, bottom, and left edge missing, right dge preserved. On the assumption that the tablet included a series of complete 12-year cycles of Jupiter the tablet had 6 years of observations on the obverse and 6 on the reverse. Col. I´ contains the reigns of Cyrus and Cambyses, col . II´ reigns of Cambyses and Darius I, cols. III´ and IV´ the reign of Darius I. The following reconstruction of this tablet was proposed by C. B. F. Walker who notes that any discrepancies between the years attested on this tablet and the dates reported by A. Sachs in LBAT, p. xxix are to be explained by the fact that the tablet was not baked and cleaned until 1978. a or u indicate intercalary Addaru or Ululu in this year. Entries enclosed in square brackets are totally lost. Thus seven complete rows of observations are lost. Whether row A is really the first row on the tablet is uncertain; if so, then the scheme began in -535/4 and ended in -498/7. lf row A is the second row on the tablet then the scheme began in -536/5 and ended in -499/8; and row L would appear at the top of the tablet and would read: L  [2]  [5]  [9]  [21]. Missing columns on the left could add 12 or 24 earlier years to the scheme.

X500056.tablet_comments: Lunar and planetary data for year 7 of Cambyses. I had the benefit of collations and comments by C. B. F. Walker; he is not responsible, however, for any errors found here.
X500056.text_comments: Obv. I 2: DIR here (and in lines 4, 6, 8) is not in the usual position for a weather-related remark like "clouds"; also, it would be the only such remark in the whole text. lt will therefore have a different meaning. I 3: there are some scatches above the number 1, but 4 bēru is impossible. ina (whatever its correct reading) here and in line 4 stands before a measure, in line 8 before a day number. Its meaning is obscure to me. Note that with the other months the interval from sunset to moonset is just listed as a number. Right edge: this column contains the Mercury data which were considered missing by Kugler. Little remains, but it is just enough to see that a last visibility in the east in the [rear] foot of the Lion was mentioned. A first visibility in the west is to follow. The next entries are broken, but the space fits to accommodate four more phases until a last visibility in the west is partly preserved for XII 19 which agrees well with computation. Rev. Some of the entries on the reverse seem to be in error, as already noted by Kugler. I refrain from correcting the text. 12: At the end of the line, "Venus above Mars" is possible only if later writing conventions are accepted: e for "above" (otherwise e-lat), and AN for Mars". This is possible if the tablet is assumed to be a later copy; but note that Mars is written dṢal-bat-a-nu in lines 9 and 16. Also, Venus was not above Mars on the date indicated. Kugler proposed to translate "maximum elongation of Venus" but could not read the signs. 19f.: eclipse of -522 Jul 17. This eclipse was rather far from being total. 21f.: eclipse of -521 Jan 10.
X500056.bibliography: Kugler; SSB I 61-74; listed as LBAT **1477

X500057.tablet_comments: Venus data from -462/1 to -392/1, arranged in 8-year-groups and 8 columns. In addition, the length of every month and the time between sunset and moonset on the first evening of the month are given. All three pieces are part of the same tablet. Each column runs from obverse to reverse and is then followed by the next column to the right. Of C, the obverse probably refers to Artaxerxes II year 5, the reverse to year 12. The astronomical information preserved fits this date, especially a close encounter of Venus and α Leonis in month III of Art. II year 5. On this tablet, two oblique wedges are used as a separation sign, especially when text spreads into an adjacent column. It is represented in the transliteration by a colon.
X500057.text_comments: IV A 15´: Venus was below η Tauri on III 14. V A 12´f.: Venus was near δ Capriecorni on this date. V A Rev. 6´: Venus was in front of β Scorpii on this date.

X500058.tablet_comments: The text refers to the year -424/3, i.e. Artaxerxes I year 40. The left side of each monthly paragraph contains the 'Lunar Three' (Sachs, JCS 2, 278; note that instead of KUR the term UD.NÁ.A is used here), the right side lists the dates of various planetary phases, one solstice, one equinox, and a rising of Sirius. The three items last mentioned are 1 day later than the dates produced by the scheme described in HAMA 362-364.
X500058.bibliography: E. Weidner, Alter und Bedeutung der babylonischen Astronomie und Astrallehre (1914), 9ff.; F. X. Kugler, SSB 2. Erg., 233-242; J. K. Fotheringham, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society 95 (1935) 719-723.

X500059.tablet_comments: Obverse: conjunctions of Mars and Moon for -422/1 to -416/5; -412/1; Reverse: conjunctions of Saturn and Moon for -422/1 to -420/19; -416/5; -403/2 to -402/1; -399/8; Left edge: list of intercalary years during the time covered by the text.
X500059.text_comments: Rev. 13´: note the rather precise time given for the end of occultation.

X500060.tablet_comments: Mars and Mercury for at least -397 to -387 and -380 to -374, respectively. The tablet originally had 5 columns on each side.
X500060.text_comments: Obv. III 2': On V 12, Mercury was above α Leonis. IV 11´: On XII 12, Mercury was near Jupiter. 34´: If 7 at the end of the line is what remains of 27, then this may be the date of Mercury passing η Piscium. V 1´ff.: the dates in this section imply an intercalary Addaru in the preceding (23rd) year. This is in contradiction to the 19-year intercalation cycle which requires an intetcalary Addaru in the 24th year or Artaxerxes II. 11´: it is possible to read ina 5 "on the 5th", but computation favors the 15th. VII 9´: The star could be θ Ophiuchi (MÚL KUR šá [KIR4 šil] ⸢šá?⸣ PA), but Mars passed above it, not below it. A possible date would be X 6. 12´: this observation of a stationary point in combination with line 14´ provides an identification of ε Piscium as (characteristic star of) ŠÍM.MAḪ. 14´ff.: while the star names in these lines are not preserved, they can be restored on the basis of computation. 18´: The name "bright one of the Bull of Heaven" for α Tauri is also attested in No. 56 B (BM 32209) rev. II 9. 24´: Mars passed β Scorpii (to which it came closer than to δ Scorpii) in the beginning of month IX; the following entry for day 14, of the same month, will have referred to passing α Scorpii. 25´: On XIII, Mars was near β Capricorni. 27´: Only the blank end of this line is preserved; the broken part most likely mentioned Mars' passing of δ Capricorni. 28´: This line must have begun the next year's observations. VIII In this column I could read so little that I did not succeed in identifying the years (assuming that it continues col. VII). A first appearance in Taurus (I. 12´) would fit year 17 of Artaxerxes III; the following entry (month IV, day 3) could refer to η/μ Geminorum. A last appearance after VII 9 (l. 10´f.) would fit year 16. Mars was near α Librae on VI 14 (l. 9´) of year 16; but the reading of this line may be wishful thinking. And Mars was not near α Scorpii on VII 9. However, most readings in this column are uncertain.

X500061.tablet_comments: Jupiter observations from year 18 of Artaxerxes II to year 13 Artaxerxes III (-386/5 to -345/4).
X500061.text_comments: I 1´: The beginning can be restored from the colophon. I 11´: the star used for reference is probably γ Arietis. IV 23´: Reading based on computation; Jupiter is "below" ε Piscium, which can be identified as ŠÍM-MAḪ in No. 59 (BM 36600+) VII 12´. Rev. I 28´: computation shows Jupiter to be 2° behind and ca. 1° below Mars, but I cannot read the traces. II 5´: only a blank space is preserved of this line. It may have contained an acronychal rising; which occurred at the beginning of month XII2. II 14´f.: these lines are restored from No. 66 (BM 35531) I 33f. III 4´: the broken part must have contained the passing of η Piscium. III 6´f.: this can be partly restored from No. 66 II 2´f.: the first appearance was not observed because of clouds, so only several days later the time between rising of Jupiter and sunrise was recorded.
X500061.bibliography: Kugler; SBB I 80ff. Tf. IV Nr. 6 (BM 35328 only). Both pieces are part of the same tablet.

X500062.tablet_comments: Mars for Artaxerxes II year 18 to Artaxerxes III year I, and Philip year 7; Venus for Artaxerxes II year 4 to 29. The Mars section probably began with year 15 of Artaxerxes II. Why a few lines of year 7 of Philip were added is obscure to me.
X500062.text_comments: I 19´: Mars passed just above δ Scorpii on V 4; tablet has šá instead of 4. 21´: On VI 2, Mars came close to θ Ophiuchi; in the beginning of line 22´, TE or DIM4 (and a measure) may have to be restored. 22´: On VI 22, Mars came very close to λ Sagittarii. 25´: three small wedges are preserved of the day number after XII2, so 6, 7 or 8 are possible. MÚL-MÚL is a guess based on computation. II 10´: there is a small space before ina UR-A; maybe the scribe wanted to add a day number later. III 3´: at the end of the line α Virginis may have to be restored. V 4´: Mars was next to χ Geminorum on this night. The reading of LÁL-tú is uncertain. The usual reading in astronomical texts is šitqultu "balance". 22´: Mars was below δ or ε Piscium at this time. Rev. I 10: unfortunately, the signs do not look like šur GIGIR šá SI. 14: in the beginning of the line, a passing of α Leonis is expected. II 3: note the designation "the middle star of the Bristle" for η Tauri; usually only the constellation name "Bristle" is used for its brightest star. 5: Venus' latitude was almost as high as that of β Tauri, so she could come very near. III 11: The rear star of the Bristle, i.e. Pleiades, would be 27 Tauri. 14: LÁL-tú here is even more obscure than in obv. V 4´; it need not be a star name. 23: Venus came near to α Virginis; on VI 10 (or later), she was below α Librae.

X500063.tablet_comments: Lunar Six, accompanied by planetary data in a parallel column, for Artaxerxes II year 26 = -378/7.
X500063.text_comments: The numerous planetary observations, a total lunar eclipse in a month XII2 and the rising of Sirius as well as the vernal equinox, give as only possible date within -600 and 0: -378/7. The data in lV 10ff. refer to Venus for the same year. II 11´: one would expect a number for "sunset to moonrise".

X500064.copy: J. Nougayrol. RA 73 (1979) 78: listed as LBAT *1396
X500064.tablet_comments: Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury for years 41 and 42 of Artaxerxes II.
X500064.text_comments: 6: "acronychal rising" error for "last appearance". 10: Venus did indeed pass closely below η Tauri on XII 3 of year 41 of Artaxerxes II. The next statement is unusual: planets are sometimes said to enter a constellation, but not vice versa. Venus came into the vicinity of β Tauri around this date, but did not reach the star. I do not know what part of Taurus might be restored in the beginning of the line. 14: The remark in the beginning of the line could be restored according to line 16, but there is less space here. 15: ina UD seems to stand for ina NIM. The appearances in the west were probably not observed, so no constellation is given. 16: The last five signs of this line are obscure to me. NIM DIB, if read correctly, reminds one of statements about position, but the text does not fit this interpretation. The sign read LUḪ also occurs at the beginning of line 18. One expects comments on the first appearance. 18: the first sign of this line is the same as the fifth from the right in line 16. It may be LUḪ, but I do not understand it. Whatever its meaning, the following ina 17 seems to be an "ideal" date. The next number "28" does not agree with computation (the other dates for Mercury in this text fit quite well); maybe it is to be read u 18, "or the 18th". If this is correct, the month name ZÍZ has to be restored in front of ina 17; note that a month was also left out in line 13. This still does not solve the problem of the first sign in this line.

X500065.tablet_comments: 3 (or originally 4) columns; on the reverse, only the rightmost column is inscribed. Tablet badly preserved.
X500065.text_comments: A meaningful translation is not possible. The remaining words may belong to eclipses or other lunar data.

X500066.tablet_comments: Mercury from year 43 of Artaxerxes II to year 16 of Artaxerxes III; Mars from year 17 of Artaxerxes III to year 2 of Darius III. According to curvature, there were 4 columms on each side, of which the two right ones are preserved. All pieces are part of the same tablet. In the transliteration of this tablet, :: represents three small oblique wedges, similar to a small 9. It occurs only after month names.
X500066.text_comments: Obv. II 12´: On III 28, Mercury was below α Geminorum. 35´: Venus was not far from Mercury during the days in question, but Mercury passed it earlier than ε Leonis. 2´´: The observation probably referred to α or β Geminorum. I 13´´: The sign at the beginning of the line looks like KIN with something written before it. II 6´: on XII 16, Mars passed α Virginis in retrograde motion. 20´: δ Scorpii has been restored here because the distance (1 cubit 4 fingers) fits. Mars came much closer to β Scorpii. 21´f.: the closest Normal star at stationary point was θ Ophiuchi. 28´: ε Piscium as characteristic star of ŠÍM-MAḪ occurs in BM 36600 VI 12´ and 14´. Here its name was probably more specific, since there is space for three or four signs before ŠÍM-MAḪ. 29´: Mars was below η Piscium, but l cannot read the traces. Maybe DUR ⸢ŠÍM-MAḪ⸣ was used. 35´: IX 4 is probably a mistake for IX 14.

X500067.tablet_comments: Mercury from year 43 of Artaxerxes II to year 16 of Artaxerxes III; Mars from year 17 of Artaxerxes III to year 2 of Darius III. According to curvature, there were 4 columms on each side, of which the two right ones are preserved. All pieces are part of the same tablet. In the transliteration of this tablet, :: represents three small oblique wedges, similar to a small 9. It occurs only after month names.
X500067.text_comments: Obv. II 12´: On III 28, Mercury was below α Geminorum. 35´: Venus was not far from Mercury during the days in question, but Mercury passed it earlier than ε Leonis. 2´´: The observation probably referred to α or β Geminorum. Rev. I 1: At the end of the line, β Geminorum is probably to be restored. II 5: at the beginning of the line β Scorpii is to be restored.

X500068.tablet_comments: Mercury from year 43 of Artaxerxes II to year 16 of Artaxerxes III; Mars from year 17 of Artaxerxes III to year 2 of Darius III. According to curvature, there were 4 columms on each side, of which the two right ones are preserved. All pieces are part of the same tablet. In the transliteration of this tablet, :: represents three small oblique wedges, similar to a small 9. It occurs only after month names.
X500068.text_comments: Obv. II 12´: On III 28, Mercury was below α Geminorum. 35´: Venus was not far from Mercury during the days in question, but Mercury passed it earlier than ε Leonis. 2´´: The observation probably referred to α or β Geminorum. 6´: the broken sign at the beginning may as well be TA, DU, or even MÚL.

X500069.tablet_comments: Both pieces are part of the same tablet; for the arrangement, see Pl. 32. There are three columns on each side. On the left edge, additional information to col. I is preserved. It may have been added Iater and come from a different source. Jupiter, Greek-letter phenomena and selected passings of Normal stars from Artaxerxes II year 43 (-361/0) to Alexander year 13 (-323/2).
X500069.text_comments: II 4´: At its stationary point, Jupiter was about 5° below η Tauri. II 7´: Note that 'Taurus' is written MÚL-MÚL at the first occurrence and GU4-AN at the second. II 20´: according to computation, Jupiter was between η and ν Caneri. III 17´: Jupiter is about 2 cubits 'behind' β Scorpii. The space in the right part of the line does not seem sufficient to restore the complete star name, so it was probably abbreviated or replaced by a suffix since the name had just been mentioned. IV 14´: On XI 10, Jupiter was above ρ Leonis; the position in line 15´ is the one at second station. Not all of the usual formula would fit into the broken part of line 14´. V 24: The four rear stars of Sagittarius are compared to the cuneiform sign ZA which consists of four wedges. This group of stars is similarly described in Diaries. VI 12´: Diary -324B 11f. and 15´ has day 28 for this appearance. 13´f.: Diary -324B 21´ gives the date III 16 and has the same distances between Jupiter and ζ Tauri.

X500070.photo: ADART 5 plate 35 ( the two pieces are not placed in their correct relative position)
X500070.tablet_comments: Mercury data, preserved for SE 6-7, but originally more.
X500070.text_comments: II 12´: This line seems to state that year 7 of the Seleucid era corresponds to year 1 of Seleucus as king. In a Diary for SE 10 (No. -302/301 rev. 21) a year 4 is mentioned, which refers to the same year count. II 13´: computation suggests month II in the beginning of the line.

X500071.tablet_comments: Mercury and Mars for years SE 7-9 (= -304/3 to -302/1): the corresponding Goal-Years would be SE 54 and 55.

X500072.tablet_comments: Mars. Obv.: Greek-Letter-Phenomena, preserved for SE 27-35 and more; Rev.: passings of Normal stars for SE 11-12, 14-16.
X500072.text_comments: Obv. II´ 3´: The year number is at least 30, but 40 or even 50 is more likely.

X500073.accession_no: Sp III 7+98 + Sp III 38 + Sp III 232
X500073.photo: ADART 5 plate 36f. (note that the join of the upper right-hand part is misplaced on the photo)
X500073.tablet_comments: Jupiter, preserved for SE 11-16, 20-25, 47-50: Mercury perserved for SE 46, 48-50.
X500073.text_comments: I 5´: Month VI error for VII. I 17´: Month III error for II. II 2: Month IX error for VIII. Rev. III 2´: "last appearance in the west" error for "last appearance in the east". III 20´: restoration of "last appearance" is based on computation; unfortunately, the following ŠÚ "west" will then have to be considered an error for "east". III 21´: ki 29 is very uncertain; only one "10" is visible, and 9 has to be assumed to be written as three wedges in three rows, whereas it is written as three oblique wedges elsewhere on the tablet.

X500074.tablet_comments: According to curvature the tablet originally was probably 3 colums wide. Obverse: Mercury for SE 14-17; reverse: Mars for SE 15.

X500075.text_comments: Obv. II 7: both 19th and 29th are possible. 19´: According to computation, this star was α Leonis.

X500076.tablet_comments: Mercury and Mars (see left edge). Mercury data are for 54-56 SE (= -257/6 to -255/4), and Mars data for 54-55 SE (= -257/6 and -256/5), so that the Goal-Years are 101-102 SE (= -210/09 and -209/8).
X500076.text_comments: II 3´: "18th" is probably an error for "8th". II 21´: "The fish" here is η Piscium.

X500077.museum_no: A 3405 (in the Tablet Collection of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago)
X500077.tablet_comments: Planetary phases ("Greek-Letter phenomena") for SE 60-70. The terminology of this text is highly abbreviated and differs from the Babylon conventions (note ABSIN0 = KI).
X500077.text_comments: Some phenomena have been restored in the translation only. Because of the chronological arrangement of the text, such restorations are certain even if just the name of a planet is actually preserved. I 1´: there is a little blanc space before the damaged number, which indicates that the line was indented, as the scribe does with eclipses. A lunar eclipse did take place in SE 60 III = -251 June 21. 17´f.: lunar eclipse of -251 Dec 14. 26´: this line should concern Venus, but the traces are not clear. II 1´f.: lunar eclipse of -250 Dec 4. 17´f.: lunar eclipse of -249 May 30. 21´: instead of 28, a reading 18 is possible. VI 1´: indentation indicates a lunar eclipse; it occurred on -243 Jan 26. VII 1´f.: lunar eclipse of -243 Jul 21. 17´f.: lunar eclipse of -242 Jan 15.
X500077.bibliography: A . Sachs, JCS 2 286f. (description): an investigation of this text by J. Steele appeared in Archive of the History of the Exact Sciences 55 (2000) 103-135.

X500078.tablet_comments: Obv.: uncertain; Rev.: Venus for SE 80-81.

X500079.copy: LBAT 1374 (35339); the other parts listed as LBAT *1375 and *1376
X500079.tablet_comments: Mercury data for 83-85 SE (= -228/7 to -226/5) and Mars data for 82-84 SE (= -229/8 to -227/6) and 50-52 SE (= -261/0 to -259/8); the corresponding Goal-Years are 129-131 SE (= -182/1 to -180/79).

X500080.tablet_comments: Jupiter for SE 97 I to 98 VII = -214/3.
X500080.text_comments: 3: The last sign in this line is erased. 4: The restoration of month VI at the beginning is based on line 5, where the ideal first visibility is placed at the end of month V (in agreement with modern computation). Therefore, the actual observation in line 4 must have occurred only in the following month.

X500081.text_comments: Obv. I´ 5´: Restore probably ". . . . in front of β Capricorni"; also in line 7´, β Capricorni will have been the reference star. II´ 23´: The time indication by ziqpu star probably refers to the occultation of Jupiter by the moon in -190 June 26.

X500082.tablet_comments: According to its curvature, the tablet originally had 6 columns. Mars data, preserved for SE 126-128 and 139-144.
X500082.text_comments: I 2´: There was a close conjunction (distance ca. 5´, i.e. 1 finger') of Mars; und Venus on -185 July 2; I do not understand what ár "behind" means here.

X500084.copy: LBAT 1378 (34624), 1380 (34877), 1381 (35255); Col. I of LBAT 1380 and 1381 is continued by col. II of LBAT 1378.
X500084.text_comments: Col. I´ concerns SE 138. It has to be a year somewhat before SE 141 (which year number is preserved in II´ 29´) that has first and last appearances of Mercury at approximately fitting dates. A first appearance in the east near Venus (I. 7´) fits only SE 138. I´1´f.: Readings and restoration based on computation. 4´: A conjunction of Mercury and Saturn is probably to be restored here. II´ 8´: 1 finger: computation suggests 1 cubit. 12´: NlM (east) error for ŠÚ (west). 14´: Month XII error for month II. At the end of the line, one could read the damaged signs ŠÚ-šú NU PAP "I did not watch its last appearance", but this does not fit into the sequence of phenomena. Col. III´ concerns SE 141 and 142.

X500085.tablet_comments: An edition of this tablet by Farouk Al-Rawi and Norbert Roughton will appear in Archiv für Orientforschung. Therefore, only a transliteration and translation is included here.
X500085.text_comments: EN occurs only in statements about Jupiter in relation to Normal Stars, and only when they are situated between acronychal rising and last appearance, i.e. when Jupiter is visible in the first part of the night. I therefore translate it by "in the first part of the night". A similar use of EN is attested in a tablet of Mercury observations from Uruk (H. Hunger, in E. Leichty et al. (Ed.), A Scientific Humanist. Studies in Memory of Abraham Sachs, p. 202). I 26: 4 1/2 KÚŠ is written in line 27, after a separation sign of six oblique wedges. II 3: the star name does not look like is le10 in line 5. II 6: error for ζ Tauri? II 9: On III 16, Jupiter is closer to η Geminorum than to μ, but still not closest. II 19: The wording does not distinguish between γ and δ Caneri, but γ fits better.

X500086.text_comments: II´: "4 cubits" is probably an error for "4 fingers"; the difference in latitude of the two planets was less than 1°.

X500087.tablet_comments: Mercury, possibly for SE 258-9. However, the position close to β Scorpii (I. 2f.) is not yet reached on VIII 12 in SE 258.

X500088.tablet_comments: Stationary points of Mercury. Note that in other observational texts, stations of Mercury are not mentioned.
X500088.text_comments: The traces of line 1´ do not seem to fit the pattern of the other lines; there are also traces of a dividing line between 1´ and 2´.

X500089.tablet_comments: Mars, Venus. The order Mars -Venus does not fit the one used by the Goal-year texts.
X500089.text_comments: While a first appearance of Mars in the end of Scorpius is not too frequent, there is no other reliable information preserved to establish a date.

X500090.tablet_comments: Both pieces are from the same tablet. Greek-Letter phenomena for several planets. The columns correspond to months; years are separated by lines on the tablet.

X500091.tablet_comments: Mercury. The terminology varies; on the whole it seems to be of relatively early date.

X500092.tablet_comments: Venus. This tablet is very badly preserved; readings are highly doubtful.

X500093.text_comments: 4´: the preserved signs are reminiscent of month names with their lengths, but then a month name should not be repeated.

X500095.text_comments: Col. I´ of this text is tentatively assigned to SE 13. This date is based on the observation of a first appearance in the east next to Jupiter (I. 4´). The only date fitting between -450 and 0 is SE 13. The other phenomena listed have sufficiently close dates. Of the positions preserved, VIII 24 does indeed show Mercury above θ Ophiuchi, albeit rather 2 cubits than 1 cubit. On V 8, Mercury was just below Jupiter.

X500097.tablet_comments: Planetary observations. Note the abbreviated star names.

X500098.tablet_comments: Mercury: traces of a further column to the right of the text.

X500099.tablet_comments: Mercury. Date uncertain; year 55 can only be Seleucid era, but the dates preserved do not fit the phenomena of Mercury in this year.

X500100.tablet_comments: Flake (of rev. ?), divided into four columns, the two outer ones blank. Mars; Mercury.

X500103.tablet_comments: Planetary observations, probably in the same sequence as the Goal-year texts. Obverse and reverse are tentatively assigned accordingly. The date (of part of the text) must be Seleucid era, during a co-regency (obv. I´ 4´ and rev. II´ 3´).
X500103.text_comments: Obv. I´ 4´: There are two periods of coregency of an Antiochus with Seleucus: SE 32 to 45 and SE 123 to 125. Of the years with 5 in the last place, only SE 125 has Venus as morning star below η Piscium in month I. Rev. II´ 9´: a first appearance must have been mentioned in the break; nothing else can follow a last appearance.

X500104.tablet_comments: Mercury, possibly (in part) for year 5 and 6 of Philip Arridaeus (= -316/317).

X500105.text_comments: Obv. 6: it is known that "becoming stationary'' is expressed by the N-stem of emēdu, but the reading here is rather uncertain. Rev. 3: The traces of the broken star name at the end of the line could be z[i], thus the beginning of some writing of zibānītu, Libra. 8: These signs are very small and their reading uncertain. PAP may have to be read ŠÚ, but I cannot suggest a translation.

X500106.tablet_comments: This text was brought to my attention by C. B. F. Walker. Its date is problematic; for instance, there is no equinox date on X 2 (I. 8) in the 'Uruk scheme' of solstices and equinoxes, which is not surprising since month X is near the winter solstice. But even apart from this, there is no fitting date for the remaining events between -450 and 0.
X500106.text_comments: I do not know the meaning of the sign transliterated ḪI. This sign, read ŠÁR, is used, often in apposition to IM "wind", in the Diaries to denote some kind of wind. This is hardly its meaning here, especially since several times we find NU ḪI, "no(t) ḪI". Also, ḪI here is far more frequent than the wind type in the Diaries. Another possible reading is DÙG "sweet, good", which also seems to be out of place. It should be noted that NU ḪI 1 occurs only on days 29 or 30 (i.e. on the last day of the month), but not in every month; in month IX, we find ḪI on day 30. The upper edge is inscribed in the direction opposite to the rest of the tablet.
